blocks.title: Addition Polymerization
blocks.text: In addition polymerization, monomers add to each other one by one, forming long chains. All the atoms from the original monomers become part of the polymer.

Nothing is lost. Monomers must have a carbon-carbon double (C=C) or triple bond (C≡C). This bond "opens up" to allow monomers to link together. No small molecules (like water) are produced as side products. This often happens through a "chain reaction" started by a very reactive molecule (an initiator, which forms free radicals).
Polyethene, a large number of ethene (CH₂=CH₂) molecules add together by breaking double bonds and linking end-to-end.

blocks.alt: Top: n CH2=CH2 + initiator, with heat/pressure over the arrow, gives [-CH2-CH2-]n; labels ethene and poly(ethene). Below: n displayed ethene, H2C=CH2 with an H on each corner, gives the bracketed displayed repeat unit -C(H)(H)-C(H)(H)- with subscript n. 'Where n is very large, e.g. up to 10 000'.
blocks.caption: Formation of poly(ethene) from ethene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 146).

blocks.text: Poly(ethene) is primarily of two types:

Low density poly(ethene) is used where a very light and soft material is needed, such as shopping bags, light plastic bottles, etc. HDPE is produced from ethene using a catalyst called Zeigler-Natta catalyst at low pressure and temperature. It finds its uses in plastic containers, thick shopping bags, toys, etc. LDPE and HDPE differ in the nature of their chains with LDPE being more branched. This makes it unable to pack tightly giving a less solid and more elastic material. While HDPE has linear chains allowing them to pack closely to give a compact structure with tough and dense material.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 'Zeigler-Natta' here. The catalyst is named after Karl Ziegler, so the spelling is Ziegler-Natta, as in the Did You Know? box.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Ziegler-Natta catalysts are a Nobel Prize-winning invention that revolutionized plastic production. It was initially discovered by Karl Ziegler in 1953. This catalyst enabled, for the first time, the low-pressure polymerisation of ethene into linear, high-density poly(ethene) (HDPE). This same catalyst family was expanded by Giulio Natta to create stereoregular polymers, such as crystalline polypropylene.
Poly(chloroethene) or PVC is made from a monomer called chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl) through an addition polymerisation reaction.
A more detailed depiction of the formation of PVC from its monomers is provided in the following scheme.

blocks.alt: Top: n CH2=CHCl + initiator gives [-CH2-CHCl-]n; labels chloroethene and poly(chloroethene) or PVC. Below: three displayed chloroethene molecules (Cl and H on one carbon, two H on the other) give a displayed chain of six carbons with Cl on every second carbon and H on all the others.
blocks.caption: Formation of PVC from chloroethene, condensed and detailed (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 147).

blocks.text: PVC is a versatile type of plastic. Its properties can be changed a lot by adding different chemicals (plasticizers).

blocks.title: Plasticizers
blocks.text: Plasticizers are chemicals added to materials to make them softer, more flexible, and easier to work with.
They cause this by reducing the strong forces between polymer chains, allowing them to move more freely.

Rigid PVC (without plasticizers) is hard and stiff and doesn't bend easily. It is chemically inert because it does not react with most acids, bases, or oils. It is a good electrical insulator. Due to the chlorine atoms, it is naturally resistant to burning and self-extinguishing. It lasts a long time and resists weathering. Plasticised PVC (with plasticisers) is flexible and soft, so it can be bent and shaped easily. It maintains good chemical and electrical properties, but is less rigid.
